newsitem.title: USA: Amoco to sell U.S. reserves and look overseas.
newsitem.headline: Amoco to sell U.S. reserves and look overseas.

text.p: Amoco Corp., the nation's fourth-largest oil company, said Monday it plans to sell 15 percent of its U.S. oil and gas properties as it focuses on more profitable ventures overseas.
Amoco did not dislose a price or the amount of overhead costs that will be reduced, or mention potential buyers.

But industry analysts said the deal could be worth up to $2.5 billion and that buyers could include Burlington Resources Inc. and Union Pacific Resources Inc., both of which have large cash balances and the ability to borrow.

The Chicago-based oil company said the assets to be sold represented 10 percent of domestic production in 1996 and one-third of its working interest properties. The properties, most of which produce natural gas, are located in Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico, Oklahoma and along the Gulf Coast.

"We are becoming more international, our strategy is to enter into proven reserves overseas, in Venezuela, Trinidad, the Nile Delta and the Caspian Sea as well as offshore Gulf of Mexico," said Amoco spokesman Jim Spangler.
In 1996, Amoco replaced 169 percent of production globally and 435 percent of overseas production, reflecting a greater emphasis on its overseas operations.

"Amoco reached a decision that the highest return on its invested capital was not going to be in the United States and they are finally putting their money where their mouth is," said Fadel Gheit, analyst at Fahenstock & Co.
Amoco's stock rose $1 to $90.375 on the New York Stock Exchange at midday.
Amoco's total reserves at the end of 1996 were 5.8 billion barrels of oil and other oil products and it produced 483 million barrels last year.
The company has already combined its Permian Basin, Texas, and Southeast New Mexico oil and gas assets with Shell Oil Co., a unit of the Royal Dutch/Shell Group.
It also plans to create a small joint venture to produce natural gas in the western United States with Maxus Energy, a subsidiary of Argentine oil company YPF SA.
"The independents can operate these sorts of fields far more efficiently than the majors. We will probably see some assets sold on to a third party," said Fahenstock's Gheit.
The Amoco deal is the latest in a series of consolidations in the oil and gas industry. On Friday DuPont Co. unit Conoco announced a $900 million deal to buy assets in south Texas.
The divestment is also part of Amoco's focus on improving shareholder value. The company recently announced a $2 billion share buyback and a 7.5 percent increase in its dividend.

The company said its most significant reserve additions in 1996 came from a large natural gas discovery in Trinidad, while its 17 percent interest in three working oilfields in the Azerbaijani Caspian Sea also added to reserves.
It has annual revenues of more than $36 billion.
The company has prequalified for the latest bidding for oil reserves in Venezuela, where it already has substantial interests.
